facts.title: Named For Russia's Atom Lab
facts.text: Flerovium honors the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions in Dubna, Russia, which in turn is named after Soviet physicist Georgy Flyorov. Flyorov is famous not only for nuclear science but for writing a 1942 letter to Stalin pointing out that physics journals had suddenly stopped publishing on fission, a clue that helped spark the Soviet atomic program. The name and symbol Fl were officially approved by IUPAC in May 2012.

facts.title: Born In A Calcium Beam
facts.text: Flerovium was first created in December 1998 at Dubna by bombarding a plutonium-244 target with a beam of calcium-48 ions. This 'hot fusion' approach, fusing a calcium nucleus into a heavy actinide, became the workhorse method for making superheavy elements. The collaboration between Russian and U.S. (Lawrence Livermore) scientists was key to confirming the discovery.

facts.title: A Member Of Element 114
facts.text: With 114 protons, flerovium sits in group 14 of the periodic table, directly below lead. That places it among carbon, silicon, germanium, tin, and lead, suggesting it could behave like a very heavy metal. Its position made it a prime test case for how chemistry changes when atoms get this enormous.

facts.title: Brush With The Island Of Stability
facts.text: Theorists long predicted an 'island of stability' near 114 protons, where certain superheavy nuclei would resist radioactive decay far better than their neighbors. Flerovium isotopes do show a hint of this: lifetimes that are surprisingly long for such heavy atoms. While no flerovium isotope is truly stable, it sits near the shore of this predicted island, making it a flagship for the theory.

facts.title: Seconds, Not Eternities
facts.text: Even flerovium's longest-lived known isotope, flerovium-289, has a half-life of only about 1.9 seconds. Most other isotopes vanish in milliseconds, decaying mainly by emitting alpha particles or by splitting apart in spontaneous fission. Studying something that disappears so fast requires detecting the chain of decay products atom by atom.

facts.title: Maybe A Noble Gas In Disguise
facts.text: Because relativistic effects make flerovium's outer electrons cling tightly to the nucleus, some scientists predicted it might be chemically inert and even behave like a noble gas rather than a metal. Experiments in the 2000s and 2010s, where single atoms were sent down gold-coated detector channels, suggested flerovium is at least less reactive than its neighbor lead. The debate over whether it is a volatile metal or nearly gas-like is still alive.

facts.title: Relativity You Can Almost See
facts.text: In flerovium, electrons near the nucleus move at a large fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's special relativity strongly reshapes the atom's structure. These relativistic effects contract the inner electron shells and alter chemical behavior in ways that simple periodic-table logic does not predict. Flerovium is one of the clearest natural laboratories for seeing relativity rewrite chemistry.

facts.title: One Atom At A Time
facts.text: Flerovium has never existed in a weighable amount; scientists have produced only a few dozen atoms in total since 1998. Each atom must be identified by its unique signature of decay energies and timings as it falls apart. This means all 'chemistry' done with flerovium is single-atom chemistry, an extreme frontier of experimental science.

facts.title: Not Found In Nature
facts.text: Flerovium does not occur anywhere on Earth or, as far as we know, in stars, supernovae, or cosmic rays in detectable amounts. It is entirely synthetic, existing only for moments inside particle accelerators. Any flerovium that might have formed in the early universe would have decayed away billions of years ago.

facts.title: No Jobs, Only Knowledge
facts.text: Flerovium has zero industrial, medical, or biological uses, and it plays no role in any living organism. Its entire value is scientific: it tests our theories about nuclear structure, the limits of the periodic table, and how matter behaves at the extreme edge of atomic size. Pursuing elements like flerovium drives advances in accelerator technology and ultra-sensitive detection that ripple into other fields.
